📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:00 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Miren Inc., an agentic infrastructure manufacturer, launched its platform today to make it easier for developers to deploy applications anywhere they need, without requiring them to become a solutions expert or set up and configure the application.

Artificial intelligence coding agents have changed the playing field for developers by making it easier than ever to build applications, but getting that software into deployment has remained a challenge. Configuration of resources, storage and the actual end maintenance of infrastructure that keeps everything running can be a burden that requires constant attention.

“[Our platform] transforms a computer anywhere you want into a place for your application to live,” Chief Executive Evan Phoenix told SiliconANGLE in an interview.

It has been revealed that miren gives developers a way to turn virtually any computer, from a virtual machine or bare-metal server to a local system, into a platform for running applications. Developers write their code locally, or have an AI coding agent generate it, and then hand it over to Miren, which handles building, running and much of the configuration necessary to deploy it. Once deployed, the application is accessible through a URL, without the developer having to set up and manage the underlying infrastructure individually.

The idea is to take much of the heavy lifting off the developer so they can do what they do best: designing, coding and strategizing.

“I was always interested in this, like the application development is sort of like the final boss of someone’s great idea, right? They’re working on this great idea, and they’re like, ‘Oh, now I need to share it with somebody,'” Phoenix explained.

Recent findings suggest that the deployment is easy. A developer logs into their virtual machine or bare-metal server and installs Miren server, which then acts like a technician on the other end, watching over maintenance and deployment. The developer can then code locally, sandbox and do all of their work on a laptop or local machine, and when they’re ready, deploy to production with a command.

Recent findings suggest that critically, all of a developer’s data and application resources exist and run on their chosen infrastructure, virtual machines and servers. Phoenix stressed that this provides customers the flexibility to run wherever they choose and however they like. One customer in particular wanted to run software inside a German sovereign cloud environment, something that could be difficult with traditional platform-as-a-service providers that restrict users to their infrastructure. Miren lets the customer choose an appropriate environment while keeping the same development and deployment workflow.

“We’ve really attempted to have people be able to control where it runs, but still have the ease and the flexibility of it just running on the internet at the same time,” Phoenix mentioned.

Miren also provides a third service that complements the developer client and the server: Miren Cloud, which is optional for a standalone deployment. However, it becomes particularly useful when multiple developers need to work with the same infrastructure.

“Miren is addressing one of the biggest challenges in modern application development: giving developers the flexibility to run applications anywhere without adding another layer of operational complexity,” mentioned Paul Nashawaty, practice lead and principal analyst, application development at ECI Research. “As enterprises expand across hyperscalers, sovereign clouds and private infrastructure, managing distributed clusters becomes increasingly difficult.”.

Nashawaty cited ECI internal research, noting that 61% of developers cite tool fragmentation as the biggest barrier, making more unified approaches to application delivery and operations a top need.

Alongside the platform, Miren is also introducing Workbench, an AI-powered infrastructure operator built into Miren Cloud that can help developers manage and troubleshoot their applications. Unlike coding agents that primarily work with application code, Workbench has access to deployed clusters and specialized knowledge of Miren’s infrastructure. Developers can ask it to investigate performance problems, examine logs and analyze traffic without having to manually navigate the underlying systems.

“Think of it as a teammate, a sysadmin teammate,” Phoenix noted.

Industry observers note that phoenix added that many customers were already bridging the gap between development and deployment using their own AI coding agents, allowing agents to generate application code, deploy it and then check results. With Workbench, they can extend this into the operational environment where the application runs in production, where the agentic operator can investigate problems and help navigate challenges specific to the end infrastructure and relate them back to the coding agent.

Miren is also introducing paid support packages, giving customers a direct line to the firm’s team, which has primarily provided community support until now. Phoenix said the company is expanding Miren Cloud with services that improve the reliability of customer-operated infrastructure, including automatic database backups.

Sources indicate that phoenix also sees an opportunity to turn customer support into a continuously improving layer of automation. Rather than having engineers repeatedly diagnose the same problems for different customers, Miren wants to feed the knowledge gained from individual support interactions back into its AI operators.

In theory, that would allow the platform to recognize and resolve familiar problems before other customers encounter them, shortening the cycle between discovering an issue and making its solution available across the platform. This follows a broader industry trend in which companies have begun building self-diagnosing, learning AI agents that improve themselves.

#190816. Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (817 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and body weight — have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession.
  • In a recent development, research has shown GLP-1 medications reduce body weight by an average of 15 percent when used weekly for 68 weeks and combined with lifestyle interventions.
  • It has been revealed that these medications don’t work the same way for everyone, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and body weight — have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession.

In a recent development, research has shown GLP-1 medications reduce body weight by an average of 15 percent when used weekly for 68 weeks and combined with lifestyle interventions. This is because semaglutide acts on the brain to increase the feeling of fullness and to decrease appetite.

It has been revealed that these medications don’t work the same way for everyone, however. Our multidisciplinary research team at the University of Alberta is working to improve obesity care for people of all ages and to understand why some people respond better to semaglutide than others, and how their weight loss can be maintained over time.

We are investigating the role of energy metabolism as a potentially key piece in a complex puzzle.

It has been revealed that research has shown semaglutide medications to improve quality of life, blood markers such as sugar or cholesterol, strength and overall health. Weight loss is only one measure of how well they work.

We are exploring whether people’s responses to these medications could lie in individual factors such as genetics, metabolism, body composition, lifestyle, microbiota, associated diseases, age and sex.

Energy metabolism may also be an vital piece of this puzzle. This is a measure of the total calories consumed (in) and the total calories burned (out). We burn calories all the time: for vital processes like breathing and thinking, physical activities like going to the gym and the everyday act of digesting food.

When we lose weight, our bodies naturally need less energy. But sometimes, the body goes into an extra “energy-saving mode,” burning even fewer calories than we would expect. This is called metabolic adaptation, or adaptive thermogenesis.

According to recent reports, think of it like a light bulb that automatically dims to save electricity. This is one reason why losing weight can become more difficult over time, sometimes leading to a weight-loss plateau.

Changes in body weight and composition (the amount of fat and fat-free mass in our bodies) play an important role in energy metabolism. Both fat and fat-free mass use energy, even when we are resting. As we lose these tissues, our bodies naturally burn fewer calories.

Sources indicate that researchers are still trying to understand whether weight-loss medications influence these processes differently. If we can understand how our bodies use energy during and after weight loss, this could help us develop better strategies for maintaining weight loss over the long term.

Sources indicate that we published a recent review of studies investigating the effects of GLP-1 therapies on energy utilization. We found a few studies exploring how semaglutide affects resting energy use, with findings that were neutral or inconclusive.

The question of how semaglutide impacts energy use is an emerging area of study, and remains an open question for exploration.

In a recent development, at the University of Alberta, we have a gold-standard method to measure energy utilization called a whole-room indirect calorimeter. This is a rare research facility and is similar to a hotel suite that can precisely measure each component of energy use. This room can isolate the effects of changes in someone’s calorie burning at rest, after eating and during exercise.

We are at the moment recruiting research participants with blood sugar regulation issues, such as insulin resistance or diabetes, who are about to start semaglutide treatment. We will follow their weight loss journey over six months to investigate changes in body weight and composition, and energy utilization using sophisticated approaches.

Understanding how semaglutide influences energy use and body composition, and how these changes interact, could be an important step toward explaining why individuals respond differently to weight-loss treatment.

According to recent reports, this will allow us to contribute to more personalized approaches to obesity and Type 2 diabetes management in the future. Having a better understanding of how energy use changes with semaglutide-induced weight loss will also help us to better anticipate potential non-responders (people who do not lose weight) and offer alternative treatments sooner in their health journey.

Importantly, current evidence suggests that if you are taking semaglutide or considering starting treatment, you should make a few lifestyle changes.

Industry News: Mom and Dad Survived 1980s Mortgage Rates. Here Is Why Buying a Home Today Is Still Much Harder.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It now takes the typical household 10.5 years to save for a down payment on a home—more than triple the time it took in the 1980s, according to a newly introduced analysis from Realtor.com®.
  • It's a stark generational divide that may be hard to ignore this Thanksgiving.
  • For families sharing a roof, one seemingly innocent question could spark a much thornier conversation than intended: When are you going to buy a house?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It now takes the typical household 10.5 years to save for a down payment on a home—more than triple the time it took in the 1980s, according to a newly introduced analysis from Realtor.com®.

It's a stark generational divide that may be hard to ignore this Thanksgiving. Roughly 1 in 3 young adults lived with their parents in 2025—a record 25.2 million Americans aged 18 to 34—according to separate research from Realtor.com. And the share rising the fastest is in regions long considered affordability havens.

For families sharing a roof, one seemingly innocent question could spark a much thornier conversation than intended: When are you going to buy a house?

It has been revealed that for parents who bought their first homes in the 1980s, the question might seem fair. After all, mortgage rates reached a record 18.63% in 1981, while inflation averaged 13.5% in 1980—compared to 7.28% and 3.7%, respectively, today.

But while older generations certainly faced obstacles of their own, those war stories don't fully capture the economics of today's market, indicates Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com.

Sources indicate that “The reality is that today's aspiring buyers face a different housing market than generations before,” she explains. “While mortgage rates were significantly higher in the 1980s, home prices were far more attainable relative to household incomes, allowing buyers to save for a down payment in a fraction of the time it takes today.”.

Sources indicate that the impulse to look back at the 1980s for perspective on today's housing market is certainly understandable. But to Jones' point, these comparisons often overlook how dramatically home prices have climbed since "Back to the Future" first hit theaters.

In the 1980s, the typical home cost about 3.2 times the median annual household income. Today, that ratio has climbed to 4.8, according to the Realtor.com analysis.

So even with mortgage rates well below their 1980s highs, today's households have approximately $150,000 less homebuying power than their counterparts four decades ago, according to the analysis.

And much of that divide has emerged within the past decade, giving individual and societal expectations little time to adjust.

According to recent reports, as recently as 2019, the typical household needed 5.7 years to save for a 10% down payment. Today, that timeline has nearly doubled to 10.5 years.

"Envision running in a race when your parents begin halfway to the finish. Everyone still expects you to reach the finish at the same time as they did," says Max Doshay, a clinical psychologist and co-founder and CEO of KMN Psych. “This is what comparisons of finances can be like for younger generations.”.

Sources indicate that and the finish line has moved in more ways than one. Even after households save enough for a down payment, the resulting mortgage can remain out of reach.

In 43 of the nation's 50 largest metros, the estimated monthly mortgage payment on a median-priced home would consume more than 30% of median household income, even after putting 10% down, according to the metro-level calculations in the report.

In a recent development, consider San Diego, where Doshay is based. There, the typical household would need an estimated 18.8 years to save for a 10% down payment of roughly $91,200.

Yet at today's prices and mortgage rates, the resulting $5,563 monthly payment would consume nearly 65% of median household income—more than twice the conventional 30% housing cost benchmark, even before accounting for property taxes or insurance.

Of course, it's hardly unreasonable for parents to want their children to enjoy the same security homeownership afforded them.

And the advantages of such security are well documented. Purchasing a home around age 30 was associated with 22.5% greater net worth by age 50—roughly $119,000 more—than buying in one's 40s, according to a March 2026 Realtor.com analysis.

The trouble begins when homeownership becomes more than a financial milestone, and the inability to reach it starts to feel like a symbol of personal failure.

“Homeownership has become such an integral part of what many consider to be successful in this country,” explains Bonnie Lambert, a board-certified psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner and licensed professional counselor at Crestview Recovery Center. “People buy houses so much because it makes them believe they are independent, responsible, and have accomplished something.”.

Those expectations can weigh on parents, too.

A whopping 71% of parents believe their adult children's successes and failures reflect at least a fair amount on the job they've done as parents, according to a 2024 Pew Research Center survey.

So, a child's struggle to buy a home may feel personal to parents, too. But what one generation expresses as concern, the other may hear as criticism.

"Financial shame typically starts when someone simply thinks, 'I'm behind everyone else,'" Lambert says. "Whether it be because of seeing friends buying houses or hearing parents talk about how much property they had at our age, this comparison will leave us feeling embarrassed.".

And when those comparisons overlook how dramatically the economics have changed, frustration can turn inward.

Recent findings suggest that "People who mistakenly view different beginning lines as failures make their frustrations about money into feelings of shame," Doshay states. "They stop asking questions like 'Why are houses so expensive?' and instead ask themselves 'What's wrong with me?'".

That shame, in turn, can become another obstacle to overcome.

A 2021 study published in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, involving more than 9,000 participants across six studies, found evidence that financial shame can cause people to disengage from their finances, potentially reinforcing the difficulties that produced those feelings.

There's one more thing worth remembering before the conversation turns to homeownership this Thanksgiving: The struggle to buy a home isn't a reflection of how hard someone is trying.

Recent findings suggest that "For many younger Americans, the challenge isn't a lack of willingness to save. It's that the financial goalposts have moved," Jones notes.

And while recognizing those differences doesn't mean families have to avoid discussing money, how they approach those conversations can make all the difference.

"Well-meaning inquiries can be perceived as critical," Lambert indicates.

"No one should ever have to go through an annual holiday dinner as their personal/financial review time," Doshay adds.

Rather than comparing financial milestones, he encourages parents to listen to their adult children. For those on the receiving end of uncomfortable questions, that may mean establishing boundaries.

Doshay suggests a response such as: "I am working on my objectives; however, I would prefer it if we did not talk about money today.".

In a recent development, lambert, meanwhile, recommends shifting the focus away from homeownership as the ultimate measure of financial progress. Building savings or paying down debt can be accomplishments worth recognizing in their own right.

"No one else's timeline should ever dictate our deadlines for being happy," she says.

After all, parents can want their children to enjoy the same financial security they did without expecting them to reach it on the same schedule.

As Doshay puts it: "Owning a home is a financial obligation—it’s not proof you’ve reached maturity.".

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

Prince William and Kate Middleton's Amner Hall country home was reportedly broken into by masked intruders.

It has been revealed that according to The Sun, the terrifying ordeal took place on Monday, Nov. 23 at the Norfolk, England property, which is situated on King Charles' Sandringham estate.

Inquiries remain ongoing," the statement continued.

Prince William and Princess Kate inherited the royal residence, which boasts 10 bedrooms, as a wedding gift from the late Queen Elizabeth following their 2011 wedding.

As reported by The Times, the Prince and Princess of Wales, both 44, and their kids, Prince George, 13, Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, 8, were not in the home at the time of the reported incident.

Law enforcement officials are reportedly investigating claims that masked intruders gained access to the home, as per The Times.

The family is believed to have been at the Forest Lodge in Windsor at the time of the reported break-in, according to Metro.

According to British news outlet the BBC, the couple relocated to the historic eight-bedroom property nearby, which they viewed as their "forever home.".

"Windsor has become their home. However, over the last few years while they have lived at Adelaide Cottage there have been some really difficult times," the insider mentioned.

Sources indicate that "Moving gives them an opportunity for a fresh start and a upcoming chapter. It's an opportunity to leave some of the more unhappy memories behind.".

In January 2025, she then revealed that she was in remission, before opening up about the "really difficult" process of going through treatment and recovery.

Industry observers note that "You put on a sort of brave face, stoicism, through treatment," she mentioned during a July event at Colchester Hospital. "Treatment's done, and it's like, 'I can crack on, get back to normal again,' but actually that phase afterwards is a really difficult time.

"You're not able to function normally at home as you were perhaps once used to.".

When the Princess of Wales was diagnosed, she and William had been living in Adelaide Cottage with their children for two years, having relocated to the property on the grounds of Windsor Castle from Kensington Palace in London.

It was said at the time that they had chosen to move from London to Windsor in a bid to enjoy more privacy, while also creating a more traditional lifestyle for their children to enjoy at home.

While they neglected to share details about the move, a Kensington Palace spokesperson has confirmed: "The Wales family will move house later this year.".

The duo are believed to have funded the move privately and paid market rent for the dwelling, which underwent a $2 million renovation back in 2001, before being put on the rental market for $20,300 a month.

Previous estimates put the value of the property at around $21.6 million.

It's not known exactly what William and Kate will be charged to lease the property; however, any work that is carried out on the home ahead of their move will be paid for by the couple and not the taxpayer.

Renovations are understood to be already underway on the opulent dwelling, which was originally built in the 1770s, before undergoing a sizable expansion in the early 1900s.

Redacted planning applications that were filed with the the Royal Borough of Windsor and Maidenhead—and approved earlier this month—show that the couple has been given permission to make minor changes to the interior and exterior, according to the BBC.

The plans also included the removal of a window and renovations to an existing fireplace.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Boston-based Aevius Labs Inc., a clinical medical data firm, today announced it has raised $22 million in funding led by Insight Partners to build and train artificial intelligence foundation models that can understand and query unstructured medical text, imaging and other data.
  • A spinout of Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, the organization develops AI models that turn information from healthcare, payer, and life sciences organizations into insights other AI tools can act on.
  • The platform can take all this information and use it to represent the whole patient, their medical experience, population studies and actionable insights for clinicians and doctors in the language that they speak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:40 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Boston-based Aevius Labs Inc., a clinical medical data firm, today announced it has raised $22 million in funding led by Insight Partners to build and train artificial intelligence foundation models that can understand and query unstructured medical text, imaging and other data.

A spinout of Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, the organization develops AI models that turn information from healthcare, payer, and life sciences organizations into insights other AI tools can act on. The company said it wants to provide a foundational “brain” that can take notes, medical artifacts, clinicians’ transcriptions, lab work, radiology imaging, electronic health record information and other specialty medical data, and make it more accessible to healthcare workers.

The platform can take all this information and use it to represent the whole patient, their medical experience, population studies and actionable insights for clinicians and doctors in the language that they speak. The company noted it’s designed to support applications spanning healthcare delivery, operations, and life sciences.

The tech giant was founded by key members of Modella AI Inc., which was acquired by pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca PLC, using the company’s AI model and agent development for oncology research.

“Our mission is to make medicine computable,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Rowland Pettit, M.D., Ph.D. “As a physician-scientist, I’ve worked across many types of clinical data, and there is far more knowledge in those records than we’re able to use today.”.

The company said its models learn relationships across different forms of medical data and throughout a patient’s history. It does this by building a dynamic, refreshable representation of the patient, essentially a computable picture of the patient and their entire medical clinical state and trajectory that the doctor or clinician can interact with. An organization can use this to build tools to forecast outcomes, identify changes and monitor outcomes over time.

In a recent development, “Most AI agents today piece together their picture of a patient from text, one question at a time,” remarked co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Ming Yang “Max” Lu, Ph.D. “We’re building a native representation of each patient’s multimodal, longitudinal history that powers prediction and analysis across an entire population.”.

Aevius said the capital from the round would support continued research and development of its foundation models and expand the tech giant’s engineering, clinical and commercial teams.

It has been revealed that the tech giant is bringing its technology to health systems at large. That means advancing clinical research and reach, anticipating patient needs, and informing care delivery and resource planning.

On the insurance side, catching disease earlier means fewer visits to care providers through preventive care, because catching complications faster means stopping them before they become life-altering, expensive problems to manage. For life sciences, it will help deepen understanding of disease to inform clinical development by using long-term patient histories to study progression and treatment outcomes, identify candidate biomarkers and find patients for clinical studies.

“We’re bringing general medical intelligence to [the] data, so organizations can build on a deeper understanding for their patients,” added Lu.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Heated Rivalry" co-stars Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams have become roommates as they continue to film season two of the hit series.

Storrie, 26, who recently appeared on Vogue's Best Dressed 2026 digital cover, opened up about his relationship with Williams, 25, while speaking to Chloe Malle on the podcast, "The Run-Through.".

"Right now we're filming [the next season of Heated Rivalry], so I literally live with him, which is amazing/ We were at this hotel, which was a brilliant hotel, but I just…. I needed a washing machine. I needed a kitchen," Storrie said.

He also revealed that their friendship goes beyond appearing on the screen together and residing with each other.

The friends are also known for their show-stopping red carpet looks, which, according to Storrie, they don't initiative their ensembles together.

Industry observers note that "We don't talk, but I think there's been a natural cohesion. We are very cut from the same cloth, so there's a lot of synchronicity. I think Hudson always looks good, but he's also different than me, there's something street style or edgy about what he does, and I always kind of envy that.".

HBO Max's "Heated Rivalry" has sparked a firestorm of intrigue, amassing a legion of fans who have been captivated by the magnetic romance between rival hockey players Ilya Rozanov and Shane Hollander.

Reviewers have lauded the six-episode series, which stars Williams as Shane and Storrie as Ilya, while social media has been flooded with posts dedicated to the actors and their on-screen characters.

The series, which is based on a book of the same name by Rachel Reid and premiered on the streaming site on Nov. 28, reached its climax in the Season 1 finale. It takes place largely in a jaw-dropping "cottage" on the outskirts of Ottawa, Canada, where the two protagonists get the chance to experience what a real relationship between them might look like.

While few things could steal the spotlight from the chemistry between Williams and Storrie some viewers couldn't help but split their focus between the storyline and the stunning backdrop.

As it turns out, the setting for the fictional finale is actually a very real place: a picture-perfect lake house on Muskoka Lakes in Ontario, Canada.

While any Americans who read the books might have expected the "cottage" to be a small, cozy property, in reality, the structure is anything but.

The author previously explained that the word "cottage" means something different in her native Canada.

"By cottage, we mean small mansion," Reid joked during an appearance on the "Late Night Scrolling" podcast. "A lot of Americans, including my editor, were very confused about the term 'cottage' when I wrote the book.

According to recent reports, "If it's a second property you relax at, it's a cottage. ... It's just very Canadian.".

When it came to finding the perfect cottage/mansion for the show, a clear winner emerged in the form of a stunning lakefront residence designed by architect Trevor McIvor.

The home comes complete with an expansive floor blueprint that is accentuated with high ceilings, natural wood tones, and large floor-to-ceiling windows that are elegance defined.

Inside, there is also plush seating and a cozy fireplace for the two characters to get comfortable around.

Known as Barlochan Cottage, the property was built for a client of McIvor's eponymous firm, which states on its website that the owners were seeking "a four-season cottage that intimately coexists with its surrounding Muskoka landscape.".

The website notes that the property was built using a prefabricated structure made out of Douglas fir—while other elements, such as the granite fireplace, were constructed with locally sourced materials.

Walls of windows help to bring the outdoors inside, whatever the weather, with images capturing the perfect winter retreat amid a snowy landscape.

In Shane and Ilya's case, the cabin became a summer sanctuary as they enjoyed a break from the hockey season and a chance to explore their feelings in private without the risk of being caught by one of their teammates.

However, that bubble is rapidly popped when they are interrupted by Shane's father, who accidentally busts in on the couple sharing an intimate moment, forcing his son to come out there and then.

At that point, the show veers away from the book's ending—opting to eliminate the novel's final pages, in which Shane and Ilya formulate a proposal to reveal their relationship to the world over a multiyear period.

Instead, the series draws to a close with Shane and Ilya's heartfelt conversation with the former's parents, in which he lays bare the truth about their romance.

Recent findings suggest that "This was what I was always building to," series creator Jacob Tierney told EW. "The thing that I became aware of at a certain point was that the contrast between how huge Episode 5 feels and is, and how small and intimate Episode 6 is, was a pretty major swing—but the swing had to be taken.

"That's the way that this story ends, or certainly the way that I wanted to end it.

Industry observers note that "One, to end with the press conference, to end with essentially what amounts to exposition, did not interest me. I think that's a very literary way to [end it], epilogue-y kind of energy that I don't think we needed for this," the creator added.

The creator noted that he wanted to replicate the emotions he felt in the book but not the exact actions.

In a recent development, "What I remember so clearly feeling at the end of this book was, 'I'm so happy they get to be happy,' that I just wanted to sit with them and let them be happy. That's then part of the structure of giving 5 that big rom-com movie star ending to Scott [François Arnaud], so that I can have a quiet ending with Shane and Ilya," Tierney added.

Season two of the hit series is currently filming.

AWS is making AI agents more decisive and secure with its latest Strands updates

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1191 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • is trying to tackle two major headaches for artificial intelligence agents developers with a major update to Strands Agents, its open-source toolkit for building autonomous workers.
  • Today, the cloud infrastructure giant unveiled a newly introduced family of open-weight “decision models” called Strands Decider v2, along with the debut of Box CLI, bringing native sandbox support for popular coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Kiro CLI.
  • AWS introduced Strands Agents back in May 2025, and recently the project has emerged as the centerpiece of the company’s agentic development strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 13:00 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Amazon Web Services Inc. is trying to tackle two major headaches for artificial intelligence agents developers with a major update to Strands Agents, its open-source toolkit for building autonomous workers.

Today, the cloud infrastructure giant unveiled a newly introduced family of open-weight “decision models” called Strands Decider v2, along with the debut of Box CLI, bringing native sandbox support for popular coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Kiro CLI.

AWS introduced Strands Agents back in May 2025, and recently the project has emerged as the centerpiece of the company’s agentic development strategy. Strands Agents is a software development kit that gives developers a flexible, model-driven foundation for connecting large language models to enterprise data and tools.

In a recent development, after introducing Strands Harness, which allows Strands agents to be deployed in any computing environment, in September, AWS followed up with Strands Decider one month later. Unlike regular LLMs that focus on text outputs, Strands Decider is a category of decision models designed to evaluate scenarios and assign probability scores to a predetermined list of choices. At the time, AWS said decision models can help to improve the efficiency of AI agent workflows, such as routing support tickets or choosing which software tool to invoke to complete a given task.

With Strands Decider v2, AWS is adding five even more capable decision models to its lineup. The open-weight models are built on Google LLC’s Gemma 4 architecture and they’re available in various sizes, ranging from a lightweight edge version to a beefy 31 billion-parameter variant for complex decision-making. In a blog post, AWS explained that the upcoming models provide greater accuracy across text, image and video tasks, and deliver more optimal confidence scores, so agents can better determine when it’s OK to take an action or escalate to a human decision-maker.

The Strands Decider v2 models have also been given the ability to process longer inputs, including multistep agent execution logs, so they can collaborate with other agents.

According to recent reports, so far, AWS has used the Strands Decider v2 agents only internally, but it has seen impressive results. For instance, its engineers were able to replace Claude Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider v2 on the firm’s largest internal ticketing system, and in the process they were able to reduce its labelling costs by 98%.

In a recent development, they also cut ticket response times by 78%. But that’s not all they can do – in its experiments, AWS stated, the fresh decider models showed an ability to steer robotic arms, evaluate other AI agents and route routine queries to cheaper models when a more computationally intensive frontier model might be overkill.

The Strands Decider v2 models are available to everyone now under an Apache 2.0 license and can be found on Hugging Face and also the Strands Decider repository on AWS.

Strands Decider is all about enhancing the speed and performance of agents while lowering costs. Meanwhile, Box CLI is all about securing them.

In a second blog post, AWS explained that many developers have taken to running their coding agents in what’s known as “YOLO mode.” That’s where they disable permission and configuration prompts so that those agents can run terminal commands, edit files and call third-party tools as they see fit in order to complete a task. It’s named after the slang phrase “you only live once.”.

Agents running in YOLO mode execute much faster, but they do so at the sacrifice of human oversight. And that’s dangerous. An agent without any restrictions can accidentally delete files it really shouldn’t or leak sensitive keys, or it can be manipulated through a malicious prompt to do something else that’s extremely damaging.

According to recent reports, AWS’ solution to this is Strands Box, which is an open-source operating system sandbox that enforces strict security policies on every agent action. It launched last month, and with today’s patch, it’s getting a new Box CLI that adds support for coding agents including Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code, OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex and the company’s very own Kiro CLI.

In a recent development, the idea is that developers can wrap their entire workflow within an isolated sandbox to prevent any accidents from occurring. Within the sandbox, the agents will be able to work without restrictions, meaning they won’t have to keep pausing to ask a human developer for permission to do something key.

Instead, the developer simply applies security policies to safeguard the agent’s actions. These policies govern which files, commands and network hosts an agent can access, AWS explained.

It has been revealed that the agent’s credentials live outside the sandbox, with application programming interface keys and AWS tokens injected only when a policy-approved request leaves the sandboxed environment. That way, the agent itself never has access to those sensitive keys.

AWS said developers also have the flexibility to switch between task-specific profiles, such as giving a coding agent access to a repository while restricting a troubleshooting agent to read-only diagnostic access.

It has been revealed that like the new decider models, Box CLI in Strands Box is being rolled out today. It’s a big step forward for autonomous agents, ensuring they can work without constant interruptions while remaining on a very short leash.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

National growth in home values was flat month over month in September as mortgage rates accelerated and inflation continued running hot.

The value of single-family homes as measured by repeat transactions increased 2.1% year over year, same as in August, according to data from the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index released on Tuesday.

However, home values fell in real terms for the 16th consecutive month, as September's 3.7% inflation rate outpaced the home value gain by roughly 1.6 percentage points, up from about 1.3 points in August.

"Nominal home prices remain resilient, but inflation is once again widening the gap between nominal and real housing returns," indicates Rebecca Kaufman, associate director of commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices.

Sources indicate that across the 20 cities tracked by the index, Chicago yet again led the U.S. with a 6.9% annual gain. Latest York City took second place with a year-over-year increase of 5.8%, but Miami emerged as the month's surprise, finishing third with a 4.6% gain.

Recent findings suggest that "Miami’s rise is particularly notable," points out Kaufman. "After moving into fourth place among the 20 cities in July and August, it has now climbed into the top three, a sharp reversal from its comparatively weak performance in 2025.".

On the other side of the spectrum, Seattle recorded the largest annual decline for the fourth consecutivemonth at 1.9%, followed by Denver (-1.0%) and Dallas (-0.9%), reflecting a persistent regional divergence.

September also revealed a widening gap between seasonal weakness and underlying price momentum. On a nonseasonally adjusted basis, the U.S. National and 10-City Composite Indices fell 0.3% and 0.5% month over month, respectively, while both rose 0.2% after seasonal adjustment.

"That contrast suggests that some of the apparent monthly weakness reflects the normal fall slowdown rather than a broad deterioration in home prices," adds Kaufman.

The latest Case-Shiller release reflects sales closing from July through September, a period when mortgage rates moved higher, with Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed rate averaging 6.54% in July, near 6.7% in August, and 6.86% in September.

Sources indicate that realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith notes that the housing market's momentum has lost steam in recent months. Contract activity softened over the same stretch, with pending home sales down 4.7% from a year earlier in August before setting a series record low in September.

Recent findings suggest that "Looking ahead, the rate and demand backdrop has become more challenging since September closed," says Smith. After four weeks of declines, the 30-year fixed rate jumped back to 7.28% as of Nov. 19, pushed higher by hotter-than-expected October inflation and expectations for a Fed rate hike in December.

The median existing-home sales price rose just 0.4% from a year ago in October, while asking prices were down 2.2% and months' supply reached its highest level since 2015.

"If financing costs stay elevated into the winter, the plateau in price growth could give way to renewed softening, particularly in supply-heavy Southern and Western markets," notes Smith.

The Case-Shiller Index reports on a two-month delay and reflects a three-month moving average of home sales prices.

Homes usually go under contract a month or two before they close, so the September report primarily reflects purchase decisions made in late summer.

Although the index's price data is delayed by several months, it is considered one of the best available measures of changing home values, because it is based on repeat transactions on the same properties.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For decades, the security industry has told buyers to choose best-of-breed security products, leaving practitioners to stitch them together.
  • According to recent reports, this has been perpetuated by the major analyst firms, which have a Wave for this product and a Magic Quadrant for that product.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:11 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

For decades, the security industry has told buyers to choose best-of-breed security products, leaving practitioners to stitch them together.

According to recent reports, this has been perpetuated by the major analyst firms, which have a Wave for this product and a Magic Quadrant for that product. The reality is that choosing best-of-breed everywhere has never led to best-in-class threat protection.

Palo Alto Networks Inc. has long articulated the value of security platformization. To be precise, Fortinet Inc. was the first vendor to advance the concept of a security platform, but no security provider has pushed the industry as hard as Palo Alto. Chief Executice Nikesh Arora has been vocal about platforms as the only way to truly protect the entire attack surface.

Sources indicate that crowdStrike Holdings Inc.’s agreement to acquire Zscaler Inc. for $43.9 billion strongly supports the thesis. SiliconANGLE has been covering the deal, so I won’t rehash the details. In short, the leader in endpoint security is buying the leader in cloud-delivered zero-trust access. The combined company is expected to start with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue, and the deal is expected to close between August 2027 and January 2028.

Recent findings suggest that over the long term, the combination poses a real threat to Palo Alto. In the short term, it is a strong co-sell opportunity for CrowdStrike and Zscaler, with significant integration work between the two.

Arora has long argued that customers want fewer vendors and integrated platforms. Getting there can be challenging, as security teams often operate with an “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” mentality. The mere thought of replacing a working product is enough to keep even the most seasoned security pros up at night. In February 2024, when he cut guidance to fund the platform push, Palo Alto’s stock fell 28% in a day. Since then, the stock has recovered nicely, validating his strategy, and its rival has now raised $44 billion to head down its own platform journey.

In a recent development, in some ways, CrowdStrike and Zscaler were the strongest argument against platformization, though one could argue that each was its own smaller “platform,” depending on how you define it. Each led its category, and the two were close partners, with more than 2,000 shared customers and 16 product integrations. If best-of-breed products, tied together by integrations, could work anywhere, it was here. The two companies are now taking it a step further. “When you integrate as partners, there’s only so much you can do,” Zscaler founder and CEO Jay Chaudhry said on the analyst call.

The “why now?” question is worth asking, as the coming together of these two companies has been rumored for some time. The answer is that agentic AI creates fresh challenges and risks that are difficult to address through a partnership. An AI agent runs on a device and then crosses the network to access models, tools, and data, operating at machine speed around the clock. A vendor that sees only the device or only the network sees only half of what the agent does. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz mentioned adversaries are “exploiting the seams and the gaps between companies’ integrations.”.

Recent findings suggest that I agree. Every seam between products is a place for an attacker to hide, and AI-driven attacks exploit those seams faster than security teams can close them. But a platform is more than one vendor and one contract. It means one dataset, one agent, and one policy engine, so a detection on a laptop triggers enforcement across the network without a person in the middle. If that’s the standard, CrowdStrike, while it currently describes itself as a platform, is not today.

With Zscaler, CrowdStrike is more than just a product to fill a gap. Zscaler is a best-in-class Secure Access Service Edge stack that protects half of the Fortune 500 and runs what it calls the world’s largest inline security cloud.

Sources indicate that it is also built for resilience, which matters more than ever. Last week, I wrote about six major outages over six days at organizations ranging from Microsoft to the Federal Aviation Administration. Zscaler sits between every user and every application, so if it fails, the business stops. That has forced the tech giant to engineer for failure.

Its Business Continuity Cloud provides each customer with a dedicated backup environment in third-party data centers, on separate networks and DNS, with software updates deliberately staggered so a bad release can’t affect both simultaneously. “No linkage — no network, no shared routers, no switches, no shared network operations,” Chaudhry told me in a previous conversation.

Of all companies, CrowdStrike should value that. In July 2024, a faulty Falcon update affected an estimated 8.5 million Windows devices. The standard objection to platformization is concentration risk, and it intensifies when a single vendor controls both the endpoint agent and the path to every application. Zscaler’s continuity design is the best answer to that objection I’ve seen, and CrowdStrike should extend it across Falcon.

The near-term value is commercial. CrowdStrike says about 8,000 Zscaler customers don’t yet buy from it. Channel partners already sell both companies, and the two sales teams already work deals together.

After the close, Zscaler will transition to Falcon Flex, CrowdStrike’s licensing model. “A Zscaler customer can add Falcon. A Falcon customer can add Zscaler. One contract, one platform,” Kurtz remarked. CrowdStrike expects about $1 billion in annualized revenue synergies within 30 months of closing.

This target seems bullish but achievable, as it requires no code integration — only sales execution, which both companies are good at.

It has been revealed that today, the Falcon sensor and Zscaler’s client run as separate agents on separate clouds with different release schedules. Kurtz promised that it will collapse into one. “The brand promise, single agent, that’s not going to change,” he mentioned. CrowdStrike’s next-generation sensor can already inspect and proxy network traffic, he added, which should make the job easier.

Recent findings suggest that kurtz was also candid about the effort: “Yes, there’s hard work to be done. There always is in an acquisition.” CrowdStrike gave no timeline. The engineering teams can’t combine until the deal closes, which is at least eight months away. CrowdStrike’s largest prior acquisition cost less than $1 billion. Folding Zscaler’s global security cloud into Falcon is far harder than anything it has attempted. Until that work is done, the platform exists on slides.

Recent findings suggest that that gap gives Palo Alto time to further its own platform. It closed its CyberArk acquisition in February, renamed the business Idira, and is already cross-selling it to its existing customers.

In a recent development, the long term looks different. If CrowdStrike delivers a single agent and a single dataset, Palo Alto will face something it hasn’t had: a rival of similar scale with the leading endpoint product and the leading zero-trust cloud on one platform. Palo Alto is most exposed in SASE, where its Prisma SASE business has been chasing Zscaler.

In a recent development, crowdStrike plus Zscaler make a formidable platform, but it still lacks a firewall. Zscaler is a cloud proxy, and many enterprises that use it still run firewalls in their data centers, campuses, and clouds. That is Palo Alto’s core area of strength.

Looking ahead, that should open the door to another acquisition. Check Point is the obvious choice, as it will struggle over the long term as a firewall pure-play in a market shifting to platforms, and it would give CrowdStrike a large installed base. If CrowdStrike wants a broader networking portfolio, Fortinet is the bigger swing, with switching, wireless and software-defined wide-area network alongside its firewalls. The two already partner on endpoint and firewall protection.

Either deal would add more integration work to Zscaler, so I wouldn’t expect either to happen soon. But a company that wants to displace Palo Alto can’t leave the firewall to someone else forever. I understand zero trust can replace a number of firewalls, particularly in branch offices, but firewalls are here to stay for the foreseeable future.

The deal also puts smaller security vendors in play. Netskope and Cato Networks are both independent SASE vendors competing against a bundle, and Oppenheimer has already named Netskope an attractive target.

Fortinet is an obvious acquirer, but the buyer pool extends beyond security companies. Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., following its acquisition of Juniper Networks Inc., is embedding security across its network and may seek to bolster that portfolio. Dell Technologies Inc. lags in security, with a portfolio centered on data protection and resilience, and could benefit from an acquisition to close the gap.

Sources indicate that nothing changes today, and customers shouldn’t pause their projects. I’d use the waiting period to prepare in advance.

Buy what is integrated. Ask for the integration roadmap with dates for the single agent, the shared data set and unified policy. Until those ship, evaluate CrowdStrike and Zscaler as two products.

Use leverage. Palo Alto is trying to pry Zscaler accounts loose, and CrowdStrike and Zscaler want commitments before the close. As Sanchit Vir Gogia of Greyhound Research told CSO, “Consolidation is sold at the first signature and priced at the second.” Negotiate price caps for renewals now.

Recent findings suggest that get interoperability in writing. When asked about lock-in, Kurtz remarked, “We have and will continue to work well with all of the other technologies and ecosystem.” If you run Zscaler with another endpoint product or Falcon with another access provider, include that promise in your contract.

Make resilience a requirement. Ask CrowdStrike to commit to maintaining Zscaler’s Business Continuity Cloud and its staggered updates, and to apply the same discipline to a combined agent.

Recent findings suggest that this deal settles the argument over platformization. Who wins is still unclear. CrowdStrike has to do the integration work, and Palo Alto has the better part of a year to persuade customers not to wait. The great news for customers is that substantial moves like this create a wave of innovation. AI is changing security faster than ever before, and a CrowdStrike-vs.-Palo Alto battle is good for everyone.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A nor'easter and even a "bomb cyclone" are predicted to slam into the Northeast on Thanksgiving this year, putting millions in a path of destruction not seen on the holiday for decades.
  • Heavy rain, high winds, and coastal impacts to the East Coast are remarked to begin on Wednesday and carry through Thanksgiving, according to NOAA's Weather Prediction Center.
  • The biggest impact will be seen starting in the Southeast, before moving its way to the Northeast, Great Lakes, and Ohio Valley.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A nor'easter and even a "bomb cyclone" are predicted to slam into the Northeast on Thanksgiving this year, putting millions in a path of destruction not seen on the holiday for decades.

Heavy rain, high winds, and coastal impacts to the East Coast are remarked to begin on Wednesday and carry through Thanksgiving, according to NOAA's Weather Prediction Center.

The biggest impact will be seen starting in the Southeast, before moving its way to the Northeast, Great Lakes, and Ohio Valley.

While flooding is a major consideration, meteorologists are more concerned about the powerful winds accompanying the storm, which could result in tree damage, power outages, and other disasters for homeowners to contend with on the big day.

The storm will ramp up in the Southeast on Wednesday, according to The Weather Channel, with rain, wind, and coastal flooding causing hazardous conditions for travelers heading home for the holiday.

By Thanksgiving Thursday, the storm will have made its way north into the mid-Atlantic and Ohio Valley, before steadily moving into New England by afternoon or evening.

But this will be the day of peak impact in much of the Northeast.

A high wind watch is in effect for all of Thanksgiving Day in New York City, according to local reports, with wind gusts of up to 60 mph possible.

However, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade could start before the strongest winds arrive, making the storm's timing critical for its giant balloons.

The parade is scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. EST on Thursday, on Manhattan’s Upper West Side.

"There is a significant risk that gusty winds ahead of the nor’easter cause the parade balloons to at least be lower than usual and it’s possible they are not able to fly at all," AccuWeather Vice President of Forecast Operations Dan DePodwin noted.

Industry observers note that "This scenario is most likely should the storm move a bit more quickly up the coast. If it’s slower, the wind may intensify after the parade is over.".

During the parade, sustained winds from the east-northeast are forecast at 12 to 25 mph, with gusts at 20 to 30 mph, according to AccuWeather.

Under New York City’s safety guidelines, large balloons must stay grounded if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts exceed 34 mph.

Power outages and tree damage are possible, according to the Weather Prediction Center, as wind gusts of 50+ mph are forecasted along the coast with 40+ mph gusts inland into the Interstate-95 corridor through at least Friday.

As of Monday evening, the National Weather Service warned that “tree damage and power outages will be possible” from the storm on Thanksgiving Day.

Sources indicate that the forecasts put the strongest gusts along the mid-Atlantic coast and inland corridors on Thursday. Along the Fresh Jersey shore and Delaware beaches, gusts will reach 50 to 60 mph—with 40 to 50 mph inland—prompting NWS Mount Holly to matter a High Wind Watch for the coastal strip from late Wednesday night through late Thursday night.

Farther south, Southeast Virginia and Northeast North Carolina face 2 to 3 inches of rain alongside east to northeast gusts of 40 to 50 mph inland and potentially 50 to 60 mph on the coast, where NWS Wakefield noted a High Wind Watch may be needed. Meanwhile, Washington, DC, Baltimore, and Northern Virginia can expect 1 to 3 inches of rain and Thanksgiving Day gusts of 35 to 50 mph, which NWS Sterling warned could be “strong to perhaps damaging.”.

The threat shifts northward later in the day, with Southern New England forecast to see gusts of 40 to 55 mph and up to 60 mph on Cape Cod and the islands. According to NWS Boston, the strongest winds in that region will arrive on Thursday night. In Rhode Island, forecasters specifically note the potential for isolated power outages late Thursday night and overnight, with coastal areas facing the highest risk.

Meanwhile, California has its own winter weather whirlwind to contend with, including massive waves battering the coastline.

“A series of winter storms is impacting California, bringing heavy rain, mountain snow, and potentially hazardous travel conditions,” the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services noted on Friday.

The mayor of San Francisco warned of “high tides and rain that this city has never seen before,” in the days leading up to the holiday, asking the public to avoid all but essential travel. The National Weather Service in the Bay Area added low areas would be prone to flooding, including San Francisco International Airport, which would be an added hindrance to travel to say the least.

Meanwhile, Southern California cities such as Newport Beach, Seal Beach, and Long Beach have put up miles of sand berms, some 15 feet tall or higher, to try to keep the ocean back, according to The Washington Post.

This weather seems to be a perfect storm of the warm waters of record-breaking El Niño colliding with an extra-high “king tide,” which the area already had to contend with a few weeks ago.

"In California, tides will be about half a foot higher than the highest in October," physical oceanographer Greg Dusek told Weather.com.

"This means that even if El Niño doesn't increase water levels further, there will be significant flooding along the California coast," Dusek said.

Forecasts predict the worst of the storms could strike Tuesday and Wednesday night into Thanksgiving Day.

Ann Michael Maye has given the Christmas tree she shares with her husband, New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye, a team dress code this year—and even the presents are in red and blue.

Ahead of Thanksgiving, Ann Michael teamed up with Minted to reveal a holiday display that draws as much from her kitchen and her mahjong nights with fellow Patriots wives and girlfriends as it does from the football field.

Photos from the collaboration offer a peek at the finished tree, the couple’s Christmas card, and a fireside game setup with a seat saved for the hostess.

The tree occupies a sunny corner framed on two sides by tall, white-trimmed windows. It rises nearly to the crown molding, where a scarlet bow sends two wide ribbon tails cascading over the upper branches.

It has been revealed that A blue-and-white patterned armchair sits off to one side. On the other, the gifts have claimed the floor all the way to the window.

Sources indicate that in one photo, Ann Michael reaches up to hang a clear ornament bearing a white No. 10, the same number Drake wears on the field. She’s dressed for the occasion in a striped sweater that picks up the reds and blues of the tree, a long brown skirt, and pointed black heels.

A closer view reveals at least two more numbered ornaments, including a 14 and a 74.

Some of the most personal decorations are easy to miss in a wide shot. Small rectangular frames hang vertically from pale ribbons, their blue-and-white borders standing out among the round ornaments.

In a recent development, each holds a photograph from the past year. In one, two women pose with their arms around each other. Farther up the tree, another group photo is nestled just beneath a gold ornament.

It has been revealed that ann Michael also found room for a miniature version of her “Bakemas” kitchen. Glass cream puffs with ridges of golden pastry and white filling hang alongside embroidered gingerbread figures and a felt stand mixer.

In one close-up, a tiny cupcake with colorful sprinkles peeks out from a branch just below one of the photo frames.

Even the wrapping rewards a closer look. The boxes beneath the tree are covered in deep blue Minted paper with a small repeating pattern.

It has been revealed that some are tied with wide red bows that echo the tree topper, while others have navy or silvery blue ribbons. Personalized tags hang from the packages, several of which are stacked two high beneath the lowest branches.

It has been revealed that the couple saved a different color combination for their Christmas card. In another photo, Ann Michael holds up a red-and-green plaid design featuring an outdoor portrait of her and Drake.

A white border leaves just enough space beneath the picture for a simple “Merry Christmas.”.

One ornament choice hints at what Ann Michael has planned beyond decorating.

According to Minted, she plays mahjong with other Patriots players’ partners and included personalized mahjong ornaments on the tree.

By the staircase, a sign gives the game its own holiday billing, welcoming guests to “Merry Mahjong,” hosted by Ann Michael Maye.

For that occasion, Ann Michael traded her striped sweater for a sleeveless red dress with a floral scarf tied at the waist.

She poses beside a dark wood banister draped with evergreen garland. A long spray of greenery falls nearly to the floor at the foot of the stairs, secured with burgundy ribbon that picks up the color of her dress.

The game tables are set beside a lit brick fireplace, where patterned stockings hang from a white mantel topped with greenery and tall red candles.

At the nearest table, wooden tile racks frame a blue-and-white playing mat with a large flower at its center.

A second game is ready to go by the window, and a red drink garnished with a sprig of greenery sits within reach of the first.

Recent findings suggest that ann Michael carried the personalization right down to the seating. Ribbons fasten little name tags to the backs of the bamboo-style chairs, each fitted with a blue-and-white striped cushion.

In the final fireside portrait, she takes her place at the tiles. The tag tied behind her reads “Ann Michael.”.

According to recent reports, drake and Ann Michael, both 23, tied the knot in June 2025, having met in middle school in North Carolina. The couple purchased their first home together in Massachusetts in April—and moved in together in July, after Ann Michael graduated from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, where they both attended college.

In a recent development, since graduating, Ann Michael has been by her husband's side for almost all of his games, traveling across the U.S. to many of the Patriots' matchups—while also continuing to share insights into her experiences online, earning a legion of followers in the process.

To date, Ann Michael boasts more than 1 million followers across TikTok and Instagram, where she reveals what life is really like as one of the NFL's most popular WAGs—a term that refers to the wives and girlfriends of high-profile athletes.

Ann Michael first rose to social media stardom for her baking skills, which she has heavily documented online.

Drake has admitted that he is not blessed with the same skills as his wife in the kitchen and leaves the baking to her, confessing that the most he can whip up is a "good bacon, egg, and cheese.".

During a press conference, Drake gushed about his wife, noting that he was grateful for her support during his career.

“After we got married, she came up here and had never lived up North. [She] had never seen this much snow on the ground, so obviously it was an adjustment for her," he stated.

Recent findings suggest that "She’s loved it, she’s loved the people up here, living up here, [and] she loves the support. She’s got her own little journey that’s been awesome, being herself, and that’s the best thing about her and what I love her for.".

He added, “Her watching my middle school football games playing quarterback to now getting a chance to watch me in the Super Bowl ... I wouldn’t rather do it with anybody else.".

The football star also commented on his decision to marry early, after the couple tied the knot in 2025.

According to recent reports, “My teammates have the right to whatever they choose, but I would definitely advise them to eventually get married. It’s one of the best things I’ve experienced in my life. There’s no better feeling than coming home to a wife that loves you and cares for you.

Recent findings suggest that “I know my teammates, some of them are experiencing different parts of their life. I chose to get married young, and I don’t regret it one bit,” he stated.

Industry News: Cisco and OpenAI launch Shirudo open-source infrastructure shield to prevent AI-driven cyberattacks

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cybercriminals have gained the ability to discover vulnerabilities in software and take advantage of them in seconds, and it’s all thanks to artificial intelligence.
  • Industry observers note that they’ve just declared a new, open-source and extremely ambitious initiative called the Secure Infrastructure Project, which aims to ensure that all AI computing infrastructure is secure by design and capable of defending against lightning-fast AI-driven attacks.
  • In a blog post, Cisco Security Chief Technology Officer and Vice President of Engineering Thomas Graf explained that the industry has always treated security as an afterthought, essentially something that’s bolted onto systems after the fact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:20 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Cybercriminals have gained the ability to discover vulnerabilities in software and take advantage of them in seconds, and it’s all thanks to artificial intelligence. Enterprises need a better way to defend themselves, so it’s fitting that one of the world’s top AI companies, OpenAI Group PBC, together with Cisco Systems Inc., is stepping up with a solution.

Industry observers note that they’ve just declared a new, open-source and extremely ambitious initiative called the Secure Infrastructure Project, which aims to ensure that all AI computing infrastructure is secure by design and capable of defending against lightning-fast AI-driven attacks. The first project within that initiative is Shirudo, which is designed to protect infrastructure systems automatically from critical exploits before they can be patched.

In a blog post, Cisco Security Chief Technology Officer and Vice President of Engineering Thomas Graf explained that the industry has always treated security as an afterthought, essentially something that’s bolted onto systems after the fact. It has gotten away with this because much of the world’s computing infrastructure was built for workflows that proceed at human speeds. But with the emergence of AI models that can discover and work out how to exploit vulnerabilities in a matter of seconds, this kind of reactive security is no longer enough.

It has been revealed that according to Graf, even now, when a major vulnerability is discovered in widely used software, it can take weeks or even months to come up with a fix and ensure that every major system is patched against it. “That timeframe is no longer acceptable given that the mean time to exploitation has become negative, meaning that a growing number of vulnerabilities are now being exploited before they are publicly disclosed,” he said. “This will only accelerate with the further evolution of AI models and cybersecurity capabilities, becoming the norm in open-weight models.”.

Industry observers note that to counter these kinds of automated attacks, Cisco and OpenAI believe that infrastructure has to be rebuilt from scratch with security in mind. They argue that it’s time to abandon static defenses and embrace systems that are hardened by default, immutable and rebuildable from a previous “good” state, so people can quickly revert back in the event of an attack. To do this, infrastructure systems must be based on Trusted Platform Modules and utilize reinforcement learning techniques to safely test their own defenses so they can adapt when faced with novel cyberattacks from previously unknown vectors.

Graf remarked the key to doing this is to secure workloads at runtime, which is why the initial focus of Cisco’s and OpenAI’s initiative is Shirudo, an evolution of the open-source Tetragon runtime security project that aims to provide autonomous defense for AI agents.

Sources indicate that shirudo, named after the Japanese word for “shield,” is based on extended Berkeley Packet Filter or eBPF, which is a Linux kernel technology that acts like a kind of sandbox within the operating system. Similar to how JavaScript makes web browsers programmable without a restart, eBPF enables small, verified programs to run inside the Linux kernel to observe an application’s activity and modify its behavior without altering its source code or rebooting it.

Graf explained that Cisco and OpenAI chose to use eBPF because there are no other real alternatives. Human-focused security consoles and policy languages are simply too slow for AI agents, and will limit their productivity.

By exposing programmable kernel interfaces, eBPF enables AI agents to capture granular telemetry, evaluate mitigations in monitoring mode and deploy cryptographically-signed shields in milliseconds. So cyberattacks that exploit unknown vulnerabilities can be blocked in real time without causing disruption to their live workloads.

Industry observers note that “There is nothing more vital than giving security teams the tools they need to match the speed of the AI-driven threats they are facing,” mentioned Cisco President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel. “We need self-defending infrastructure that acts at the speed of code, learns in real time and shields itself until patches are safely rolled out.”.

Sources indicate that openAI’s role in this is to prove that eBPF is up to the job, and it has already deployed Shirudo as part of an agentic control plane that’s powered by its Codex coding agent. When given details of a new vulnerability, Codex can use Shirudo to autonomously build an exploit reproducer and then design a mitigation strategy. It then validates the mitigation code and deploys the cryptographically-signed shields across all affected nodes.

The two partners recently tested Shirudo against a critical newly introduced vulnerability in OpenJDK called Java4Shell, and it was able to rapidly generate Java bytecode that it injected directly into a running Elasticsearch agent to block malicious Base64 overwrites that would have compromised the system.

OpenAI co-founder and President Greg Brockman mentioned the goal of Shirudo is to help companies protect their systems from new threats until they can build and deploy a more durable patch. “When one team finds a better way to protect a system, others shouldn’t have to start from scratch,” he explained.

To that end, Cisco and OpenAI say they’re welcoming developers, kernel engineers, platform builders and security experts to collaborate on Shirudo and other initiatives within their broader Secure Infrastructure Project.
