Key insights from HPE’s Q4 earnings report

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1649 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.delivered a record fiscal fourth quarter this week, roughly doubling its fiscal 2027 growth outlook, but its stock gave back nearly all of the prior day’s rally.
  • According to recent reports, fourth-quarter revenue rose 50%, to $14.5 billion, orders grew 88%, and adjusted earnings of $1.43 per share topped the high end of guidance.
  • Recent findings suggest that I joined a briefing with Chief Executive Antonio Neri and a small group of independent analysts shortly before the results came out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:27 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

It has been revealed that hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.delivered a record fiscal fourth quarter this week, roughly doubling its fiscal 2027 growth outlook, but its stock gave back nearly all of the prior day’s rally. The selloff suggests Wall Street still prices HPE as a low-margin server vendor, even though the results describe a networking and artificial intelligence infrastructure company with demand exceeding its ability to ship.

According to recent reports, fourth-quarter revenue rose 50%, to $14.5 billion, orders grew 88%, and adjusted earnings of $1.43 per share topped the high end of guidance. HPE now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to grow 27% to 35%, with adjusted earnings of $5.05 to $5.35 per share, according to its earnings release.

Recent findings suggest that I joined a briefing with Chief Executive Antonio Neri and a small group of independent analysts shortly before the results came out. Here are my four takeaways for investors and information technology leaders:.

Neri explained that networking orders grew more than 4.5 times faster than networking revenue in the quarter, up from 3.5 times the quarter before, and HPE exited the year with $10.5 billion in AI backlog.

According to recent reports, HPE doubled its networking purchase commitments over the summer and raised them again in the fourth quarter, but those components carry lead times of 28 to 40-plus weeks, so Neri expects networking conversion to pick up starting in the second quarter. Supply constraints are a better problem to have than weak demand, but they mean fiscal 2027 hinges on converting orders rather than winning them.

The Juniper Networks integration is complete, and the annual cost-synergy target has risen to $800 million, but the bigger story remains the profit mix. Chief Financial Officer Marie Myers said networking will account for more than 40% of HPE’s operating profit by the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, up from less than a quarter of revenue. AI is a major driver, with routing orders growing by triple digits as customers connect AI data centers to one another.

Security was the soft spot, which Neri called “just timing.” When I asked whether the security portfolio is where he wants it as the industry consolidates around big platforms, he argued for a different path.

In a recent development, “Fortinet and we have a different strategy — the convergence of security and networking — and we are taking it all the way down to the silicon level,” he stated. The convergence of networking and security is underway but will take time to execute, as a considerable amount of technical debt must go through its depreciation cycle. In a greenfield situation, organizations can easily deploy a converged solution, but in a brownfield environment, it requires much more work. This is the right strategy, but it remains a “prove-it” business for HPE.

Industry observers note that many neoclouds rely on vendor financing and chip-backed debt, raising real concerns about who is left exposed if the buildout slows. HPE notes it has stayed out, and Neri was quite emphatic about it on the briefing.

“I want to be clear: We have not financed any neocloud through HPFS, our financing arm,” he mentioned. “We have zero exposure to any AI financing for neocloud.” HPE has likely left some revenue on the table, but it drew the line in the right place. It will sell to neoclouds, as its $1.2 billion Vultr order indicates, without acting as their bank. Enterprise and sovereign customers account for the majority of its cumulative AI orders, and if the neocloud financing chain breaks, HPE’s financing arm won’t be the one holding the paper.

Training built the first phase of AI infrastructure, and Neri believes inference will build the next and will dominate demand for AI infrastructure. “I believe by the end of the decade, 80% will be in AI inferencing,” he mentioned. “Much of that will land on-prem. Much of that will be distributed, for sure. That’s why the server business is structurally well-positioned.”.

Recent findings suggest that once agents are in production, token costs become a recurring bill, and companies will want inference running alongside their own data. Those servers require far more memory and pull in storage and services, which is better business than racking graphics processing units for a hyperscaler.

Evidence of this is the interest in Helios, the Advanced Microdevices Inc. rack that uses HPE’s Ethernet switching rather than Nvidia’s proprietary interconnect. I asked Neri whether Jensen Huang’s brief departure from Nvidia Corp. had opened that door. He said interest was building before then, as customers look to diversify.

According to recent reports, HPE shares jumped 17% on Monday ahead of the report as part of a broader AI rally, then fell about 13% in early trading on Tuesday, ending near where they started the week. I see three reasons for this.

Recent findings suggest that the first is margins. Cloud & AI operating margin was 18.4% in the quarter, and HPE guided to about 14% for fiscal 2027. Reuters reported that JPMorgan analysts called margin mix the key debate for investors.

It has been revealed that the second is pricing. Myers said higher selling prices have been the biggest driver of server growth, and she expects gross margin to moderate in the second half as AI server volumes ramp and costs rise faster than pricing.

The third is timing. HPE expects about 54% of revenue in the second half, with the ramp tied to Helios shipments, the Oracle Corp. deal, customer data center readiness and component supply. Those are fair execution questions, but they miss the shift in where HPE’s profit comes from.

In a recent development, on the topic of margins, the 18.4% came off an unusual stretch of favorable pricing that should not have been modeled as permanent. Neri argued the guide is still “significantly higher than any historical margin we have had in this business,” and he’s right outside the past year. A year ago, the segment’s margin was 9.3%. Margin rate also isn’t margin dollars. At 30% to 40% revenue growth, my math highlights Cloud & AI adding well over $1 billion in operating profit at the midpoint.

Industry observers note that the bears are right that price-driven server growth doesn’t warrant a premium multiple, which is why the mix matters more. The market is fixated on the segment whose margins are normalizing and ignoring the one whose margins are expanding. Adjusted earnings per share are still guided to grow by 27% to 35%, in line with revenue growth. That’s far from the margin doom-and-gloom narrative on the stock.

It has been revealed that the back-half concern is real but manageable. Myers described the pipeline as multiples of the backlog, and Neri said the guide assumes only historical win rates against it.

In a recent development, then there’s quality. HPE is guiding to about 30% growth and at least $5.5 billion in free cash flow, has no neocloud financing exposure and has already brought leverage below its target. It trades at about eight times the midpoint of its adjusted earnings guidance. “I don’t see us at a multiple that is 8 to 9x; it makes no sense whatsoever,” Neri stated on the earnings call.

Sources indicate that for old HPE, that’s true, as it’s a server vendor, but HPE is increasingly a network vendor each quarter. In fact, during our pre-call with Neri, he led with networking and spoke at length about the business before pivoting to the server business. Expect networking to continue to drive a larger share of profits.

Fiscal 2027 is an execution year. HPE must convert purchase commitments into shipments, ramp Helios and prove that networking margins can climb even as cloud and AI margins settle. I’ll be watching networking order conversion more closely than server margins. If HPE executes, today’s multiple will prove to be too low.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Compass International Holdings may have filed 16 separate antitrust lawsuits against 16 separate MLS, but according to court documents filed earlier this week, those MLSs are seeking to combine these lawsuits into one.

In a recent development, in a motion filed on Monday to stay the lawsuit Compass filed against it, California Regional MLS (CRMLS) told the court that it and the other MLSs Compass has filed lawsuits against have asked to consolidate or coordinate the pretrial proceedings for the various Compass v. MLS lawsuits currently pending across the country in federal court in the Southern District of New York (SDNY). If the panel declines to select New York, the motion identifies the Western District of North Carolina and the Middle District of Florida as alternative venues for the consolidated litigation.

According to the motion, the MLSs have also asked to include the two declaratory judgement lawsuits nine MLSs have already filed against Compass in the SDNY.

Industry observers note that “Compass has chosen to wage the same legal fight in courts across the country, creating unnecessary costs and the risk of conflicting rulings,” Richard Haggerty, the CEO of OneKey MLS, mentioned in a statement. “Each of the 16MLS organizations are challenging that approach. We believe these cases belong before one judge, and we will continue defending the cooperation rules that ensure no brokerage gains an unfair advantage by withholding publicly marketed homes from the shared marketplace.”.

This request comes after Compass informed the SDNY court that it prepares to file a motion to dismiss the declaratory judgement lawsuits or to sever and transfer each MLS’s claims to the district where Compass has brought its own antitrust case against that MLS.

After months of posturing and clashes over policies, the legal dispute between Compass and the MLSs kicked off in earnest this September when Compass sent letters to MLSs across the country demanding that they stop fining agents for publicly marketing office exclusive listings. Later that month, Compass CEO Robert Reffkin told a room full of MLS executives gathered at the Council of MLSs (CMLS) that he would sue any MLS that refused to give in to Compass’s demands.

Despite Reffkin’s threats, it was actually CRMLS that made the first move, filing a lawsuit in early October seeking a declaratory judgment that its policies on listing cooperation are “fair, procompetitive, and legally sound,” according to a company announcement. CRMLS has since been joined by New York’s OneKey MLS in this lawsuit, while MLSListings, Arizona Regional MLS, bridgeMLS, Canopy MLS, REcolorado, Hive MLS, and Doorify MLS have filed their own lawsuit, also in the SDNY, seeking the same judgements as CRMLS and OneKey.

In the midst of these lawsuits hitting the court docket, Compass filed its own lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging that its rule unlawfully restrict how homeowners and their agents can publicly market properties outside the MLS.

Roughly a month later, Compass reiterated those same claims in 15 separate lawsuits filed against 15 MLSs. MLS defendants in those lawsuits include bridgeMLS, Bay East MLS, Contra Costa MLS, MLSListings, The MLS-CLAW, San Diego MLS, Canopy MLS, Hive MLS, Doorify MLS, Arizona Regional MLS, Recolorado, NorthstarMLS, Houston Association of Realtors, Stellar MLS and OneKey MLS.

In an emailed statement a Compass spokesperson told HousingWire that the filing is “a procedural request  that does not change the substance of [Compass’s] claims.”.

“Each MLS applies its own rules, and the impact of those rules on agents, home sellers, and buyers is specific to its local jurisdiction,” the spokesperson added.

It remains to be seen if court will allow the MLSs to consolidate their lawsuits. This is not the first time real estate industry defendants have sought to consolidate similar lawsuits. Several real estate brokerage defendants in the copycat commission lawsuits attempted to consolidate their cases, but their request was rejected.

#190696. Tech Report: What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1542 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1542 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.
  • Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Recent findings suggest that ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He stated he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

In a recent development, his co-founder, Jessica Chestler, mentioned music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be mentioned for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Sources indicate that megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

Sources indicate that “I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan remarked. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

In a recent development, jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

According to recent reports, “Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he mentioned. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Sources indicate that daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

According to recent reports, natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she remarked, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova remarked. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

It has been revealed that for mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Recent findings suggest that andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney noted.

According to recent reports, she leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

Recent findings suggest that hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he notes, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Recent findings suggest that rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

Recent findings suggest that “In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

Recent findings suggest that she played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea indicates she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

Industry observers note that marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

Recent findings suggest that his Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein mentioned.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

It has been revealed that “Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he stated. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

Recent findings suggest that on setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Recent findings suggest that bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Recent findings suggest that kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she remarked.

Recent findings suggest that as for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

According to recent reports, so the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova mentioned, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

NEAR Protocol Revenue Rises Despite 50% Token Sell-Off

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (498 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today.
  • NEAR Protocol (NEAR) fell 11.41% on Nov.
  • Over the same period, the volume of NEAR Intents went up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

NEAR Protocol (NEAR) fell 11.41% on Nov. 20 and traded at $2.84, according to TradingView data. In early October, the token was trading near $6, and it has lost about half of its value since then.

Over the same period, the volume of NEAR Intents went up. "NEAR went from $6 to $3 in about a month. funny thing is, NEAR Intents is doing more volume now than it did in october," NEAR ecosystem contributor Evgeny Haenko wrote on X on Nov. 20.

According to Haenko, NEAR Intents averaged around $129 million in daily volume in October, and in November it was processing around $134 million a day. "The price got cut in half, the business didn't slow down at all. hard for me to be bearish here," he wrote.

Recent findings suggest that NEAR Intents lets people swap assets across more than 30 blockchains, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and XRP. The service is built into wallets such as Ledger, Trust Wallet and Brave. Over the past year, its trading volume grew 7.1 times to $39.5 billion.

NEAR Intents has collected about $63 million in fees in total, and the network keeps about 29% of that amount. Fees on the NEAR Intents interface, payments from B2B partners and the spread on better-than-market trades accounted for 16.3%, 9.9% and 2.8% of the fees, respectively. Over the last 30 days, the protocol earned about $1.8 million, compared with $2.2 million in October.

Recent findings suggest that since February 2026, the protocol has used NEAR Intents revenue to buy NEAR on the market. More than 1.84 million NEAR have gone to the buyback wallet so far, and that is 41.6% of all distributed onchain revenue. Base transaction fees on the network are burned in full.

According to recent reports, in early November, the NEAR community also voted to cut the maximum annual issuance from 2.5% to 1.6% over two years. The proposal, HSP-029, went through House of Stake, NEAR's governance initiative, and Haenko is one of its participants.

On Sept. 29, Bitwise rolled out the first U.S. spot NEAR ETF on NYSE Arca under the ticker NRR. Two days later, on Oct. 1, NEAR Intents paused its services after an exploit that cost about $3.8 million, and the team promised to compensate users in full. The exploiter later returned the funds. "The funds from the $3.8M NEAR Intents hack were sent back in full," NEAR Intents general manager Alex Shevchenko noted at the time.

#190693. Mortgage rates whiplash is in full effect, with jumbo loans shedding 25 bps this week

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (870 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Mortgage rates whiplash is in full effect, with jumbo loans shedding 25 bps this week

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The seesaw pattern for mortgage rates that’s been the story for much of the second half of 2026 reared its head again this week as rates for major loan types declined, reversing some of the increases from prior weeks.
  • At HousingWire‘s Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, rates for 30-year conforming loans averaged 7.53% — down 5 basis points from a week ago.
  • Rates in the mid-7% range continue to weigh on homebuyer demand and affordability metrics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The seesaw pattern for mortgage rates that’s been the story for much of the second half of 2026 reared its head again this week as rates for major loan types declined, reversing some of the increases from prior weeks.

At HousingWire‘s Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, rates for 30-year conforming loans averaged 7.53% — down 5 basis points from a week ago. Rates for 30-year loans through the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) dropped 7 bps to 7.30%, while rates for 30-year jumbo loans plummeted 25 bps to 7.62%.

Rates in the mid-7% range continue to weigh on homebuyer demand and affordability metrics. Last week’s application index from the Mortgage Bankers Association revealed that total applications were down 5% on a weekly basis. MBA data released Tuesday found that affordability is about 8% weaker than a year ago, even though it improved slightly from September to October.

Industry observers note that “Higher mortgage rates weighed on application activity last week, with the 30-year fixed rate rising to 7.35%. Purchase applications were down 18% from a year ago, reflecting continued affordability challenges and softer homebuyer demand. The direction of mortgage rates in the coming weeks will be key to the housing market’s momentum heading into 2027,” MBA president and CEO Bob Broeksmit stated in a statement.

Dan Ribler, vice president of capital markets and strategy at national reverse mortgage lender Longbridge Financial, remarked that the October jobs report should’ve sent rates higher. Nonfarm payrolls increased by 165,000 positions last month and the unemployment rate remained steady at 4.1%, indicative of today’s healthier labor market conditions in relation to 2025.

Ribler noted that the jobless rate has been below 5% every month since September 2021, unemployment claims are lower than a year ago and the Federal Reserve‘s “own description is the labor market is very strong.” But strong employment trends have been overshadowed by stubborn inflation, which continues to run well above the central bank’s 2% annualized target.

“Inflation has been above 2% year over year 57 months in a row,” Ribler remarked. “The Fed has, by the way, under this administration, reiterated the 2% hurdle and that they’re going to be tough on inflation. They’re certainly talking the hawk talk, saying we’re going to keep inflation under 2%.

“But man, I don’t know about you, if my kid breaks curfew 57 nights in a row — and I say I’m going to punish you one of these times and I never do anything about it — at some point, he stops believing me, right?”.

Inflation is likely to prompt the Fed to raise rates next month. The CME Group‘s FedWatch tool reveals that a 25-bps hike in December is all but certain, with 96% of interest rate traders saying that the federal funds rate will rise to a range of 4% to 4.25%. It was last at that level in September 2025.

Much of the housing and mortgage industry headlines in the past week have cast a shadow over any potential market improvements in 2027.

Selma Hepp, chief economist at Cotality, noted in a statement that existing home sales have fallen to their lowest level since August 2010. She also pointed to a Realtor.com analysis, which found that the typical repeat buyer will pay about $1,100 more per month if they choose to sell and move.

“A meaningful housing recovery requires rates to come down and, importantly, stay down long enough to improve affordability and unlock turnover,” Hepp stated. “Until then, the adjustment is likely to come through weaker sales and softer home prices rather than widespread homeowner distress.

“The number worth writing is the $1,100. That’s the jump in monthly payment a typical repeat buyer takes on just to move house. It’s the clearest explanation yet of why nobody is selling.”.

Industry observers note that newly introduced home sales have been equally grim, with September’s seasonally adjusted annual rate of 676,000 sales representing a 5.3% decline from a year ago. Higher rates have also prompted homebuilders to remain cautious about creating more supply, with U.S. Census Bureau figures showing that single-family housing starts were down 3.2% year over year in September. Monthly gains in total starts were largely tied to the multifamily sector.

“Challenging affordability has been weighing on the resale market. Newly pending sales fell 17% in October, the largest year-over-year drop since 2023,” Zillow senior economist Kenny Lee said in a statement. “Single-family homebuilders have been navigating the same challenge. While homebuilders have been adapting to the softer market by offering concessions and building smaller homes, the 2027 spring home-shopping season could see a slow start as buyer demand continues to wane.”.

The relative lack of sales has weighed on mortgage origination volumes, with ATTOM data for the third quarter of 2026 showing that the roughly 730,000 purchase loans closed during that period were the lowest figure for any third quarter in 14 years.

Refinance activity was also bleak, with the roughly 561,000 refis in Q3 down 19% year over year. Refi lending was down from Q2 2026 in nearly 90% of the metro areas analyzed by ATTOM, with the largest declines in major metros like San Jose, San Francisco, Dallas, Austin and Louisville, Kentucky.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

According to recent reports, why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026.

It has been revealed that AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

According to recent reports, why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

Sources indicate that krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

In a recent development, they eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

It has been revealed that that opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein demonstrates you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

Industry observers note that the firm announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Compass International Holdings is presently in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this massive news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Famous financial educator and author of "Rich Dad Poor Dad" Robert Kiyosaki has disclosed when investors should begin accumulating Bitcoin (BTC) during the current cryptocurrency market bloodbath.

While he is consistently bullish on Bitcoin, Kiyosaki is asking investors to be patient and not buy the flagship cryptocurrency before the current crash ends.

Recent findings suggest that in his latest X post on Nov. 20, Kiyosaki shared an vital investment lesson and warned his followers against catching a falling knife.

"Never grab a falling knife," Kiyosaki warned.

The financial guru suggested that this means investors should wait until the cryptocurrency market crash ends before buying more Bitcoin.

"That means wait for the crash to end….before buying," Kiyosaki elaborated.

Notably, Kiyosaki shared that he began buying Bitcoin when its price was around $20,000 after another major market crash.

The best-selling author hinted that he is planning to do the same during the current market downturn.

"Will wait for Bitcoin bottom again," Kiyosaki noted.

The financial educator reminded his followers of one of his notable investment tips.

"Your profit is made when you buy….not when you sell," Kiyosaki noted.

Basically, the financial educator suggested that investors should prioritize finding good entry prices rather than trying to buy Bitcoin while its price keeps dropping.

However, Kiyosaki did not specify a Bitcoin price target or how he is going to know that the market has bottomed out.

Kiyosaki's remarks follow another devastating Bitcoin crash that took the flagship cryptocurrency to its lowest level in more than four months.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 20, the world's largest cryptocurrency crashed below the key psychological price level of $60,000 for the first time since July.

In a recent development, according to Reuters, Bitcoin crashed to around $59,381. Bitcoin shed over 3% in a single trading session.

Interestingly, BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) saw a record $541.1 million in daily outflows.

Overall, the latest data shows that November has seen total net outflows from U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs worth around $3.47 billion.

Interestingly, Kiyosaki has shared his excitement about buying Bitcoin during major market corrections several times.

Earlier, on Nov. 20, Kiyosaki described the ongoing market crash as a possible buying opportunity. He suggested that experienced investors are sitting back and waiting to accumulate while bad investors are trying to sell everything.

"I am most excited about Bitcoin's crash. Waiting to buy more," Kiyosaki declared.

It has been revealed that kiyosaki stressed that Bitcoin has a limited supply of 21 million coins. He believes that this scarcity makes Bitcoin vastly different from traditional government-issued currencies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Valuable Records are Available for Free Online.

SILVER SPRING, Md. , Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The National Genealogical Society (NGS) is excited to share that the Preserve the Pensions project to digitize War of 1812 pension files is finished, and the files are now available to the public for free permanently with full-text search via Fold3.

Recent findings suggest that the culmination of sixteen years of fundraising and careful work to save deteriorating files and make them accessible online, this project provides genealogists and family historians with nearly three million pages of records from approximately 90,000 individual files. A partnership between NGS, Fold3, Ancestry, FamilySearch, and the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), and contributions from people and organizations across the genealogy community, made this incredible endeavor possible and illustrate the power of collaboration.

In a recent development, "After successfully raising the $2.7 million needed to conserve and digitize the War of 1812 pensions deposited with NARA in Washington, DC, we are thrilled that our digitization partner, Fold3, has completed digitizing the last box of pensions. This effort, originally initiated as a request from the National Archives, concludes the largest private/public partnership the genealogical community has had where donations led directly to making these invaluable records freely available," mentioned NGS President David E. Rencher, AG, CG, FUGA, FIGRS, FNGS, FSG. "We thank all who have donated to the project and to those of our partners and the many genealogical societies who spearheaded efforts to raise the funds needed, particularly the Indiana, Illinois, and Fairfax, Virginia, Genealogical Societies.".

War of 1812 pensions provide information on a generation between the Revolutionary War and the 1850 census, which is the first census to provide the names of individuals in a household. The files may include an affidavit from the soldier or widow including where he enlisted, where he served, and for how long. The widow may state their date of marriage, when he died, a Bible record which may include the names and birth dates of children, and affidavits from other relatives which may help prove family relationships. Sometimes the information about the widow or an affidavit from her will disclose her maiden name. These files may also contain other meaningful military records and information on a person's fellow veterans or neighbors.

It has been revealed that "These records are extremely valuable to researchers and historians, and we are proud to be a part of this project. We're grateful for the efforts started by the Federation of Genealogical Societies before it merged with NGS in 2020, and it has been an honor to carry this forward and continue the work with our partners to see it to completion," mentioned NGS Executive Director Matt Menashes, CAE.

"The project serves as a template for future initiatives illustrating that together, the genealogical community can help preserve and make available vital genealogical records for generations to come. These records may be used not only for genealogy, but also for those studying history and as part of a school curriculum for students," stated Rencher. "Thank you to all who made this possible!".

NGS offers an online course, War of 1812 Records, for anyone wanting a deeper understanding of how to interpret these records and what other records might add to the story. The modules guide participants through War of 1812 military records, historical context, and research strategies. More information and registration can be found on the NGS website.

Access the War of 1812 pension files via Fold3 and learn more about the project's completion on their blog.

SOURCE National Genealogical Society.
